lesson.menu_title: Phrasal Verbs in Action -- When Contracts Fall Apart or Come Together
lesson.menu_desc: The life of a deal told the way people actually say it -- 31 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Phrasal Verbs in Action
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Paula Teodoro Valdivia | Lesson 9 -- Phrasal Verbs in Action

listenings.text: I have worked with lawyers from about fifteen countries, and there is one thing I noticed early, and it took me years to understand what I was hearing. Their English was excellent. Technically perfect. And it was strange. Not wrong. Strange. They spoke the way a contract is written. The agreement was executed on the twelfth of March. The supplier subsequently terminated the arrangement. Nobody in an American office talks like that. We say: we drew it up on the twelfth. They backed out in June. And here is the part that surprised me. I always assumed that formal language sounded like authority. It does not. It sounds like distance. When somebody speaks to me in written English, I hear a document, not a person, and I stop asking questions, because it feels like there is nobody there to ask. So my advice is simple, and it is not about being casual. Keep the Latin verbs for the page. On a call, use the two word verbs. Same meaning, different room. You will sound closer, and people will interrupt you, which is exactly what you want.

For about eight months I said two things wrong, every week, in front of the same people. I said back out the deal, and I said draw up it. Nobody corrected me. Not once. They understood me perfectly, so why would they? I only found out because I recorded myself for a different reason and heard it. That was not the useful part, though. The useful part was what I changed afterwards. I had been studying phrasal verbs the way everybody does, from a list, in alphabetical order. Back out, break down, call off, carry out. Fifty of them on a page. I could recognize all fifty and produce none of them, because a list has no situation in it, and my mouth needs a situation. So I stopped. Now I learn them inside one story. The story I use is a deal. Somebody draws it up, we carry it out, we iron out the open points, the term rolls over, someone backs out, the thing falls through. Once a week I tell that whole story out loud, from the first draft to the collapse. Six months of that, and the verbs come when I need them.

extra_audio.text: Their counsel drew up the first version in March. We carried out our part and sent the annex over in April. Then one liability clause held it up for two months. In the end the supplier backed out, and the deal fell through.
